title: Weather and festivals
goal: Talk about the weather, get to know the Basque festival calendar, and give or accept invitations.
bekal: describe the weather with three different patterns: *egiten du*, *ari du*, *dago*
recognize the big festivals of Euskal Herria and the greetings that go with them
invite, accept, and politely decline invitations

dialogs.title: Elkarrizketa — Aste Nagusia dator
dialogs.intro: Early August in Bilbo. Unai walks into the apartment carrying a blue scarf printed with the name of his group.

lines.speaker: Unai:
lines.text: Budi, datorren astean Aste Nagusia da!
lines.id: Budi, next week is Aste Nagusia!
lines.literal: Budi, coming week-in Week Big-the is!

lines.speaker: Unai:
lines.text: Bilboko jai handiak. Bederatzi egun kalean.
lines.id: Bilbo's big festival. Nine days out in the streets.
lines.literal: Bilbo-of festival big-the(pl). nine day street-in.

lines.speaker: Unai:
lines.text: Kontzertuak, dantzak eta su artifizialak gauero.
lines.id: Concerts, dances, and fireworks every night.
lines.literal: concert-pl, dance-pl and fire artificial-pl night-every.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Amazing! Will the weather be good?

lines.speaker: Unai:
lines.text: Ez dakit. Abuztuan euria egiten du batzuetan.
lines.id: I don't know. In August it sometimes rains.
lines.literal: not I-know. August-in rain-the doing it-has sometimes.

lines.speaker: Unai:
lines.text: Primeran. Gure konpartsan egongo gara, plaza ondoan.
lines.id: Great. We'll be at our group's tent, next to the square.
lines.literal: great. our group-at be-will we-are, square side-at.

lines.speaker: Unai:
lines.text: Ezer ez. Poza eta gogoa besterik ez!
lines.id: Nothing. Just good spirits and enthusiasm!
lines.literal: anything not. joy and desire other-any not!

notes: **Weather has three patterns, and you have to learn all three as they are.** *Euria **egiten du*** (it rains, as a weather habit), *euria **ari du*** (it's raining right now), *eguraldi ona **dago*** (the weather is good). The most common mistake: using *da* — *euria da* isn't a Basque sentence.

**Berdin dio — doesn't matter.** Literally "it says the same". Similar expressions: *ez dio axolarik* (it's not important), *berdin zait* (it's all the same to me), *ez da ezer* (it's nothing). All are used to reassure someone or let a small thing go.

**Konpartsa — the heart of Bilbo's festival.** During Aste Nagusia, the squares fill with big tents run by *konpartsak*, local clubs that each have their own name, colors, and music. Anyone can walk in. It's not a festival to watch but one to join — which is why Unai's answer to "what should I bring?" is "nothing".
**Gora …! — long live …!** A cheer you'll hear at every festival and every match: *Gora Bilbo!*, *Gora euskara!*, *Gora gu!* The opposite is *behera* ("down"), but you'll rarely need it.

blocks.text: With egin: weather as a habit or forecast
With ari: weather happening right now
With egon: the state of the sky

blocks.title: Sirimiri — the region's signature rain
items: *Zirimiria* (in Spanish *sirimiri*) is a fine drizzle that can fall all day without ever really soaking you — and without ever really stopping. It's the most typical weather on the northern side of Euskal Herria.
That's why umbrellas are rarely used; locals just pull up their hoods and keep walking.
The southern side (Araba, Nafarroa) is much drier and hotter in summer. So "Basque weather" is really two different climates, separated by a mountain range.

blocks.text: *Olentzero* deserves a special mention: instead of Santa Claus, Basque children wait for a chubby charcoal maker who comes down from the mountains on Christmas Eve. He's pictured smoking a pipe, wearing a beret, and loving his food. This figure is much older than Christmas itself.

*Sentitzen dut* literally means "I feel it" and is used just like "I'm sorry" in English — both to turn something down gently and to offer condolences. Don't mix it up with *barkatu*, which is for apologizing for a mistake or getting someone's attention.

blocks.title: Festival customs worth knowing
items: At street festivals, everyone stands and moves around; sitting at one table all night isn't the local way.

Drinks are paid in rounds, not split: one person pays for the whole round, then the next person takes a turn. Offering to pay separately comes across as a bit stiff — but nobody will be offended if you explain that you don't know the custom yet.
The *kuadrilla* — a fixed group of friends for life — is the most important social unit here. Being brought into a kuadrilla is a far bigger sign of acceptance than a simple invitation.
